data.text:
Studying emotion theories through connectivity analysis: Evidence from generalized psychophysiological interactions and graph theory

Yun-An Huang, Jan Jastorff, Jan Van den Stock, Laura Van de Vliet, Patrick Dupont, Mathieu Vandenbulcke. NeuroImage 172 (2018) 250–262. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuroimage.2018.01.026

Psychological construction models of emotion state that emotions are variable concepts constructed by fundamental psychological processes, whereas according to basic emotion theory, emotions cannot be divided into more fundamental units and each basic emotion is represented by a unique and innate neural circuitry.

Sixteen healthy volunteers (8 females, mean age 25 years, range 23–32 years) participated in the experiment. All participants were right‑handed without neurological or psychiatric history and without any medication at the time of the experiment. This study was approved by the Ethical Committee of the University Hospitals Leuven and all participants gave written informed consent in accordance to the Declaration of Helsinki.

In brief, the whole stimulus set contained 30 stimuli displaying a walking avatar with four types of expressive emotion (angry, happy, fearful and sad) and one emotionally neutral type. During the task, participants were asked to press a button to judge whether the stimulus was emotional or not. The experiment consisted of 8 runs and each run contained 60 trials in which a stimulus was shown (12 trials per condition: angry, fearful, happy, sad, neutral) and 12 baseline fixation trials. In each trial, the stimulus was shown for two gait cycles. A trial lasted between 2 and 4 s, due to the different movement speeds of each motion clip. A fixation trial with a fixation dot displayed on a black screen lasted 3 s. The inter‑stimulus interval varied between 2300 ms and 5000 ms determined by an exponential random variable.

All brain images were acquired using a 3T MR scanner (Intera; Philips Medical Systems) with a 32 channel receive‑only head coil at the University Hospitals Leuven, Belgium. Functional images were acquired using gradient‑echo planar imaging with the following parameters: 37 slices; sequential slice acquisition order; 0.3 mm interslice gap; voxel size: 2.75 × 2.75 × 3 mm³; repetition time: 2 s; echo time: 30 ms; flip angle: 90°; SENSE accelerate factor 2. A structural whole brain three dimensional high resolution T1‑weighted image was acquired using an MPRAGE sequence with parameters: matrix size: 256 × 256; 182 coronal slices with 1.2 mm thickness; repetition time: 9.7 ms; echo time: 4.6 ms; inversion time: 900 ms; SENSE acceleration factor: 2.5.

The general emotion network (GEN) was reported in our previous study and comprises regions involved in core affect, conceptualization, language and executive control. We obtained the peak coordinates of those regions in GEN that were at least 12 mm apart. The ROIs were defined as spheres positioned in each peak coordinate with a 6 mm radius. Consequently, we obtained 61 ROIs.

All functional data were analyzed with SPM12 (Wellcome Department of Cognitive Neurology, London, UK), and in‑house developed scripts for computing information flow indices and classification of the four emotions. The functional connectivity results were mapped on the brain using the BrainNet Viewer toolbox (Version 1.53, Beijing Normal University, Beijing, China). All software was running on Matlab (version 2013b, The Mathworks, Inc. Natick, MA).

All functional images were processed using the following five steps: (1) Slice timing correction; (2) Realignment to correct for small head movements; (3) Coregistration between the mean functional image and the structural image; (4) Warping the structural image to MNI‑space and applying this transformation to the individual functional images with a voxel size of 2 × 2 × 2 mm³ in MNI space; (5) Spatial smoothing using a 3D isotropic Gaussian kernel with FWHM = 8 mm.

The 8 experimental parameters were formed by the onset times of angry, happy, fearful, sad, neutral, baseline, left and right button pressing, respectively. We then defined 5 main contrasts: “general emotion > neutral”, “angry > neutral”, “happy > neutral”, “fearful > neutral” and “sad > neutral”. At the second level, we performed a one‑way ANOVA between the contrast images from the 4 contrasts from the individual analysis: “angry > neutral”, “happy > neutral”, “fearful > neutral” and “sad > neutral”.

We applied the information flow analysis to the gPPI matrix to obtain information flow indexes, namely outdegree, indegree, totaldegree and directionality. A positive directionality indicates that the ROI behaves like a “source”, whereas a negative directionality indicates that the ROI behaves like a “receiver”.

Supplementary data related to this article can be found at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuroimage.2018.01.026.
